theme: राज्य और भोग / Victory, kingdom, and pleasure lose their pull
context: Arjuna turns the warning into a direct moral question: if the objects he wants—victory, rule, pleasure, and life itself—are not worth the loss of those he loves, then the whole framework of the battle collapses under the weight of relationship.
contextHindi: अर्जुन अब इस चेतावनी को सीधे नैतिक सवाल में बदल देते हैं: अगर वे चीज़ें, जिन्हें वे चाहते हैं—विजय, राज्य, सुख, जीवन—उन लोगों के नुकसान के बराबर भी नहीं हैं, जिनसे उनका लगाव है, तो पूरी युद्ध-योजना ही रिश्तों की कीमत पर निष्कर्षहीन हो जाती है।
sanskritDevanagari:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च |
किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा ||१-३२||
transliteration:
na kāṅkṣe vijayaṃ kṛṣṇa na ca rājyaṃ sukhāni ca .
kiṃ no rājyena govinda kiṃ bhogairjīvitena vā ||1-32||

wordByWord.meaning: I desire, I seek; the desire is not absent, but it has been stripped of illusion.
victory; in the battle context, the achievement of success as a political and military end.
kingdom, sovereignty, rule; the political reward of winning.
pleasures, comforts, enjoyments; the living rewards and comforts that accompany power.
what is the use, what is the purpose; the rhetorical question exposes the emptiness of the ordinary aim.
by kingdom, through rule; the gain is weighed against the human cost.
Govinda, Krishna; Arjuna calls Him by a beloved name, not simply as a commander.
with enjoyments, through worldly pleasures; the pleasures that seem attractive in abstract become trivial in face of kinship.
with life, by living; even the ordinary continuation of life seems doubtful against this moral cost.
or; the question opens a wider comparison between different forms of gain.

spokenHindi:
अर्जुन अब सीधे कहते हैं—‘न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण’—मैं विजय नहीं चाहता, कृष्ण। ‘न च राज्यं सुखानि च’—न राज्य चाहता हूँ, न सुख। ‘किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द’—हमें राज्य से क्या लाभ, गोविन्द? ‘किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा’—भोगों से क्या, जीवन से भी क्या? यह श्लोक बहुत गहरा है, क्योंकि यह सिर्फ एक सैनिक की हार नहीं है; यह एक व्यक्ति की आत्म-तुलना है, जो पूछता है कि अगर अपने प्रियजनों का नाश करना पड़े, तो राज्य, भोग और जीवन की सार्थकता कहाँ रहती है?

यहाँ समझने की बात यह है कि अर्जुन का प्रश्न केवल ‘विजय’ का नहीं है; वह यह देख रहा है कि व्यक्ति की इच्छाएँ किस तरह अपने वास्तविक मूल्य को खो देती हैं, जब वे मानवीय बंधनों को टुकड़े-टुकड़े करने के लिए मजबूर हों। राज्य, भोग, जीवन—ये सब चीज़ें अपने-अपने स्थान पर अच्छी लगती हैं, लेकिन जब उनके पीछे अपने लोगों की हानि खड़ी हो, तब उनका मूल्य बदल जाता है।

इस श्लोक में बड़ी महत्त्वपूर्ण बात यह है कि अर्जुन अपने ‘विकल्पों’ को मूल्याकंन कर रहे हैं, न कि अपने ‘दायित्व’ को झुठलाने के लिए। वे यह नहीं कह रहे हैं कि ‘कुछ भी नहीं है’; वे यह कह रहे हैं कि ‘जिस चीज़ का मूल्य ही नहीं, उसके पीछे अंधा दौड़ना सही नहीं है।’
clearEnglish:
This verse is a dismantling of the ordinary logic of success. Arjuna is not merely saying, “I do not want to fight.” He is saying that the objects usually considered desirable—victory, rulership, pleasure, and even life itself—lose their weight when the cost is the destruction of one’s own kin. The question is not rhetorical decoration; it is a direct challenge to the moral worth of the very aims that drive a conflict.

The crucial point is the contrast between gain and relationship. In ordinary life, people often imagine success as something clean and separable from the people around them. Arjuna’s insight is that success is never morally neutral when it requires the disintegration of love, loyalty, and family. This is why the verse is more than a battlefield complaint: it is an ethical test of what counts as true gain.

A modern lesson is simple but strong: before chasing status, comfort, or worldly success, ask whether it is worth the relationships, self-respect, and peace it may cost. If the answer is no, the aim itself must be reconsidered.

interpretationPerspectives.label: Text
interpretationPerspectives.explanation: The verse explicitly says Arjuna does not desire victory, kingdom, or pleasures, and asks what use they are when the cost is the loss of one’s own kin.

interpretationPerspectives.label: Commentary
interpretationPerspectives.explanation: The DLS reading frames this as the moral collapse of ordinary ambitions when they are weighed against love, duty, and human bonds.

interpretationPerspectives.label: Inference
interpretationPerspectives.explanation: A reasonable inference is that ambition becomes ethically hollow when it depends on harming those whose lives and love matter most to us.

practicalApplication.label: Measure real gain
practicalApplication.text: Before saying yes to a goal, ask: what will it cost in relationships, peace, and integrity, and is that price acceptable?

practicalApplication.label: Reclaim perspective
practicalApplication.text: When success is being pursued at any cost, pause and ask whether you are chasing a reward or hiding from a deeper moral question.

reflectionQuestion: What ambitions in my life seem attractive only because I am not yet counting their human cost?
reflectionQuestionHindi: मेरी जीवन में कौन-सी आकांक्षाएँ आकर्षक लगती हैं क्योंकि मैं अभी तक उनके मानव-प्रति की कीमत नहीं गिन रहा हूँ?
